rationale: B wins because it gives the same core facts sharper protagonists and stricter kill gates. Its line, "The people who run Discord servers are about to find out if their communities will pay," is a real human story; A's "Discord opens a paid tier inside community servers built on free membership" is the flatter product-frame version. A is strong, but B is better at saying what must be proven before anyone bothers a reporter.
gaps_in_A: "Discord servers have historically been free communities" is plausible, but not in the supplied facts. Verify it or soften it.
"Substack's 10%, Patreon's tiers" and "Discord, Patreon, Twitch, Geneva" add outside context the update did not supply. Fine if checked, sloppy if not.

"Discord turns 200M users into a payments business ahead of a reported IPO" risks overclaiming the IPO posture and the size of the monetizable base. The set flags this, but the headline still pushes hard.
gaps_in_B: "unpaid volunteer community managers" and "people they've been moderating for free" are good copy, but not grounded in the update. Do not smuggle color in as fact.

"The prevailing belief is that a 200-million-user base plus a cheap take rate is an obvious win" is explicitly inferred, which is honest, but still needs external proof before pitching the contrarian angle.
"Discord takes 10% where Apple takes 30%" narrows the supplied "app-store standard" to Apple. It works as shorthand, but mobile billing mechanics decide whether it survives.
The `newsjack-detector` next step is a little too eager. The launch itself is already a peg; checking for a live app-store hook is useful, not mandatory.
